conclusions: There is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ extending the one we have on $K$

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 1
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2) and Remark \ref{dpidpj}, $$\mathbb{D}':=\left(D_{p\mathbf{j}}|_C\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}$$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-derivation on $C$. Let $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}:C\cong C^{1/p}$, and $\mathbb{D}''$ be $\mathbb{D}'$ transported to $C^{1/p}$ using $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}$. Then $\mathbb{D}''$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ and by the construction it has the required properties (see also Lemma \ref{transport} and the proof of Proposition \ref{strictext}).
nodes.statement_short: Transport the induced g[m-1]^Fr-derivation (D_{pj}) on C to C^{1/p} via the inverse Frobenius.

nodes.name: Induced action on C
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2) and Remark \ref{dpidpj}, $$\mathbb{D}':=\left(D_{p\mathbf{j}}|_C\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}$$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-derivation on $C$.
nodes.statement_short: D_{pj} restricted to C is a g[m-1]^Fr-derivation.

nodes.name: Transport to C^{1/p}
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}:C\cong C^{1/p}$, and $\mathbb{D}''$ be $\mathbb{D}'$ transported to $C^{1/p}$ using $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}$. Then $\mathbb{D}''$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ and by the construction it has the required properties (see also Lemma \ref{transport} and the proof of Proposition \ref{strictext}).
nodes.statement_short: Transport along inverse Frobenius gives the required derivation.

nodes.name: Rings R and R'
nodes.statement: We consider the following rings (the set $B$ indexes the variables): $$R:=K\left[X_b^{(\mathbf{i})}\ |\ \mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^{\times e},\ b\in B\right],$$ $$R':=K\left[X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\ |\ \mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e},\ b\in B\right];$$ where for each $b\in B$, $X_b$ is identified with $X_b^{(0,\ldots,0)}$. We put a $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R$ which is $\mathfrak{g}$-extending $\mathbf{K}$ in the following way: $$D_{\mathbf{j}}\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{i})}\right):=\sum_{\mathbf{f}\in [p^m]^{\times e}}c^{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}X_b^{(\mathbf{f})}.$$ Then $R'$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-subring of $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Define polynomial g-rings R, R' with D acting on variables via structural constants.

nodes.name: W, Psi and m
nodes.statement: Let us define a subset $W\subset R'$ as follows: $$W:=\left\{\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)\ |\ \mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e},\ b\in B\right\}.$$ We define the following $K$-algebra map $$\Psi:R'\to C^{1/p},\ \ \Psi\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)=D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)^{1/p}$$ and let $\mathfrak{m}=\ker(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define W, the map Psi to C^{1/p}, and m = ker Psi.

nodes.name: m is a maximal g[m-1]-ideal
nodes.statement: By Claim 1, $\Psi$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-map, so $\mathfrak{m}$ is a maximal $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-ideal of $R'$ containing $W$.
nodes.statement_short: By Claim 1, m is a maximal g[m-1]-ideal containing W.

nodes.name: Goal: J prime
nodes.statement: We will show that the $\mathfrak{g}$-ideal $J$ in $R$ which is $\mathfrak{g}$-generated by $\mathfrak{m}$ is prime (then we can take $L$ as the field of fractions of $R/J$).
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show the g-ideal J generated by m is prime.

nodes.name: Orderings
nodes.statement: Let us order the set $[p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ as $\mathbf{k}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{k}_{(p^{(m-1)e})}$ such that for $i\leqslant j$, we have $|\mathbf{k}_{(i)}|\leqslant |\mathbf{k}_{(j)}|$ (in particular $\mathbf{k}_{(1)}=(0,\ldots,0)$). We also order $B=(b_s)_{s<\kappa}$ such that $b_0=a$.
nodes.statement_short: Order multi-indices by degree and B with b_0=a.

nodes.name: Claim 2 block
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 2} \\ There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types: $$\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum _{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{t,i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})};$$ where $b\in B$, $s<\kappa$, $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, $j\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}$ and $\alpha_{i,l},\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}\in K$. \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim 2] We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps. In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators. In Step (0,2), we consider two cases. \\ Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators. \\ Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators. In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$. Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 2 and its proof: triangular generators of m.

nodes.name: Claim 2: triangular generators of m
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 2} \\ There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types: $$\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum _{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{t,i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})};$$ where $b\in B$, $s<\kappa$, $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, $j\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}$ and $\alpha_{i,l},\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}\in K$.
conclusions: There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps. In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators. In Step (0,2), we consider two cases. \\ Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators. \\ Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators. In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$. Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transfinite step-by-step construction of generators, splitting on whether D_{pk}(b) lies in the field generated so far.

nodes.name: Stepwise construction
nodes.statement: We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps. In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators. In Step (0,2), we consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Build generators in steps; first step adds X^p-b_0.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators.
nodes.statement_short: If D_{pk}(b_0) is new over K^p(b_0), add a p-th power generator.

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise add a linear generator.

nodes.name: Next steps
nodes.statement: In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate with the enlarged field.

nodes.name: Complete the construction
nodes.statement: Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Continue for all multi-indices and all b_i.

nodes.name: Reduce operators to apply
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{hsideal}, it is enough to apply to the generators from Claim 2 the operators $D_{\mathbf{i}}$, where $\mathbf{i}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ or where $\mathbf{i}$ is of the form $(p^{m-1})_i$ (see Lemma \ref{hsideal} for the definition of $(p^{m-1})_i$). If $\mathbf{i}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ then we get elements of $\mathfrak{m}$, so we may focus on the other case. To treat the first type of the generators from Claim 2, we just need to use that there is $\mathbf{l}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ such that $\mathbf{i}=p\mathbf{l}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.33 only finitely many operator types need checking.

nodes.name: First-type generators
nodes.statement: We obtain the following: \begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl} D_{p\mathbf{l}}\left(\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)\right) & = & \left(D_{\mathbf{l}}\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{l}}\left(D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)\right) \\ & = & \left(\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}} c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}X_b^{(\mathbf{k})}\right)^p - \sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}} (c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}})^pD_{p\mathbf{k}}(b) \\ & = & \sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}} \left(c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}\right)^p\left(\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{k})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}}(b)\right), \end{IEEEeqnarray*} where the second equality holds by Remark \ref{dpidpj}, since $b\in C$. Hence we get that $D_{p\mathbf{l}}((X_b^{(\mathbf{j})})^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b))$ belongs to the ideal generated by $W$ in $R'$, so it also belongs to $\mathfrak{m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Operators map first-type generators into the ideal of W, hence into m.

nodes.name: Second-type generators
nodes.statement: After applying $D_{\mathbf{i}}$ to the second type of generators, by Lemma \ref{newton} we get the following: $$D_{\mathbf{i}}\left( X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})} \right) = $$ $$ {\mathbf{k}_{(j)}+\mathbf{i}\choose \mathbf{i}}X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)}+\mathbf{i})} + \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}d_{i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)}+\mathbf{i})}\right)^l + Q,$$ for some $d_{i,l}\in K$, where $${\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\choose \mathbf{i}}:={i_1+j_1 \choose i_1}\cdot \ldots \cdot {i_e+j_e \choose i_e},$$ and where $$Q\in K\left[X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{r})},\ X^{(\mathbf{j})}_{b_s}\ |\ t<s,\ \mathbf{r}\in [p^m]^{\times e},\ \mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}\right].$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute D_i on second-type generators via Lemma 3.14.

nodes.name: Triangular form of J
nodes.statement: We forget now about the HS-differential structure on $R$ and $J$. The obtained set of generators of $J$ is of the form $J_1\cup J_2$, where $J_1\subseteq \mathfrak{m}$ and $J_2\subseteq R'[X_{\gamma}]_{\gamma\in \mathcal{I}}$ (after renaming variables), and $$\mathcal{I}:=\kappa\times \{1,\ldots,e\}\times (\mathbf{k}_{i})_{i\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}}$$ with the lexicographical order. Moreover, there is a subset $\mathcal{I}_0\subset \mathcal{I}$ such that without loss of generality (since $p$ does not divide ${\mathbf{k}_{(j)}+\mathbf{i}\choose \mathbf{i}}$), we have $$J_2=\{X_{\gamma}-Q_{\gamma}\ |\ \gamma\in \mathcal{I}_0\},$$ where for each $\gamma\in \mathcal{I}_0$, $Q_{\gamma}\in R'[X_{\delta}]_{\delta<\gamma}$.
nodes.statement_short: The generators of J are triangular in new variables.

nodes.name: J is prime
nodes.statement: Therefore, the ring $R/J$ is isomorphic to a polynomial ring over $R'/\mathfrak{m}$, so the ideal $J$ is prime.
nodes.statement_short: R/J is a polynomial ring over the field R'/m, so J is prime.

nodes.name: Idea of the proof; strict iff differentially perfect
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof above may seem to be technical, but the idea is very simple. For $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, the value $D_{\mathbf{j}}(a^{1/p})$ is determined by Claim 1. For $i\leqslant e$, we set $D_{(p^{m-1})_i}(a^{1/p})$ as a new formal variable. The values of the remaining operators on $a^{1/p}$ are determined by the $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity rule. \item \item The above proof may be also used to show that a $\mathfrak{g}$-field is strict if and only if it is \emph{differentially perfect}, i.e. each of its differential extension is separable. This generalizes a result of Kolchin (see Chapter II, Section 3., Proposition 5.(a) in \cite{kol1}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: values

nodes.name: g-ring structure on tensor products
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-rings. Then there is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R\otimes_kS$ such that the natural maps $\mathbf{R}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-homomorphisms.
conclusions: there is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R\otimes_kS$ such that the natural maps $\mathbf{R}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-homomorphisms
nodes.label: forap

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.36
nodes.statement: It is convenient to show a more general result. Assume that $V,W$ are schemes over $k$ and $\mathbb{D}_V$ and $\mathbb{D}_W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on $V$ and $W$ respectively. As in the case of the usual group actions, we get a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V\times W$ such that the projections $V\times W\to V,W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-invariant. By considering the affine schemes and dualizing, we get what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Product of g-schemes carries a unique compatible action; dualize for affine schemes.

nodes.name: Generalize to schemes
nodes.statement: It is convenient to show a more general result.
nodes.statement_short: Prove a general statement for schemes.

nodes.name: Diagonal action
nodes.statement: Assume that $V,W$ are schemes over $k$ and $\mathbb{D}_V$ and $\mathbb{D}_W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on $V$ and $W$ respectively. As in the case of the usual group actions, we get a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V\times W$ such that the projections $V\times W\to V,W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: The product V x W gets a unique compatible action.

nodes.name: Dualize
nodes.statement: By considering the affine schemes and dualizing, we get what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Dualize for affine schemes.

nodes.name: Amalgamation over strict g-fields
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}_1,\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}_2$ be $\mathfrak{g}$-field extensions and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is strict. Then $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ can be $\mathfrak{g}$-amalgamated over $\mathbf{K}$ into a $\mathfrak{g}$-field.
conclusions: $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ can be $\mathfrak{g}$-amalgamated over $\mathbf{K}$ into a $\mathfrak{g}$-field
nodes.label: lambdaap

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.37
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, we can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are separably closed (since separable algebraic extensions are \'{e}tale). Then $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is a subfield of $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Remark \ref{defgen}(5), it is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subfield. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} (using Corollary \ref{dimconstants}), the $\mathfrak{g}$-field structure on $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is strict. Therefore we can assume that $K$ is separably closed as well. \\ The proof will be finished exactly as in \cite[Prop. 2.6]{Zieg2}. We can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are subfields of a big field $\Omega$ and that they are algebraically disjoint over $K$. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}, the extension $K\subseteq L_1$ is separable. Since $K$ is separably closed, this extension is regular (see \cite[p. 367]{lang2002algebra}). By \cite[Thm. VIII 4.12]{lang2002algebra}, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$, thus $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ is a domain. By Lemma \ref{forap}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ extending those on $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext} again, we get the required $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on the field of fractions of $L_1\otimes_KL_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to separably closed K, then as in Ziegler: regular extensions are linearly disjoint, so the tensor product is a domain carrying a g-structure.

nodes.name: Reduce to separably closed L_i
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, we can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are separably closed (since separable algebraic extensions are \'{e}tale). Then $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is a subfield of $L_1$ and $L_2$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG L_1, L_2 separably closed, containing K^sep.

nodes.name: K^sep strict
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{defgen}(5), it is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subfield. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} (using Corollary \ref{dimconstants}), the $\mathfrak{g}$-field structure on $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is strict. Therefore we can assume that $K$ is separably closed as well.
nodes.statement_short: K^sep is a strict g-subfield, so WLOG K separably closed.

nodes.name: Ziegler's argument
nodes.statement: The proof will be finished exactly as in \cite[Prop. 2.6]{Zieg2}. We can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are subfields of a big field $\Omega$ and that they are algebraically disjoint over $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Ziegler: place L_1, L_2 algebraically disjoint in a big field.

nodes.name: Tensor product is a domain
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}, the extension $K\subseteq L_1$ is separable. Since $K$ is separably closed, this extension is regular (see \cite[p. 367]{lang2002algebra}). By \cite[Thm. VIII 4.12]{lang2002algebra}, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$, thus $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ is a domain.
nodes.statement_short: Separable over separably closed means regular, so linear disjointness makes the tensor a domain.

nodes.name: g-structure on tensor
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{forap}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ extending those on $L_1$ and $L_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.36 gives a g-structure on the tensor product.

nodes.name: Extend to fraction field
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext} again, we get the required $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on the field of fractions of $L_1\otimes_KL_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to the fraction field by etaleness.

nodes.name: g integrable to a formal group law
nodes.statement: In this subsection, we assume that $\mathfrak{g}$ is of the form $W[m]$ for a formal group law $W$ (see Remark \ref{intgs}).

nodes.name: p-th root function lambda
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p$ and $\lambda$ be the following \emph{$p$-th root function}: $$\lambda:K\to K,\ \ \ \lambda(x)= \begin{cases} x^{1/p}\text{ for }x\in K^p, \\ 0\ \ \ \ \text{ for }x\notin K^p. \end{cases}$$

nodes.name: Language L^lambda
nodes.statement: Let $L^{\lambda}$ be the language of rings expanded by a unary function symbol $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Language L_{e,m}
nodes.statement: Let $L_{e,m}$ be the language of $k$-algebras (so there are constants in the language for the elements of $k$) with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations.

nodes.name: Language L^lambda_{e,m}
nodes.statement: Let $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}=L^{\lambda}\cup L_{e,m}$.

nodes.name: Natural L^lambda-structure of fields
nodes.statement: Each field of characteristic $p$ has a natural $L^{\lambda}$-structure and we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item A field extension $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension if and only if $L^p\cap K=K^p$. \item If $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L_{e,m}$-extension and $\mathbf{K}$ is strict, then $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-extension. \item Suppose $R$ is a subring of a field $L$, $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$ and $R\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. Then $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: Each field of characteristic $p$ has a natural $L^{\lambda}$-structure
A field extension $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension if and only if $L^p\cap K=K^p$.
$\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-extension
$K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension
nodes.label: lamb

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: The item $(1)$ is clear and $(2)$ follows from Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(2). The last item follows by an easy computation.
nodes.statement_short: (1) clear; (2) from separability in Lemma 3.22(2); (3) by computation.

nodes.name: Elementary extensions of separably closed g-fields
nodes.statement: Let us assume that $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-fields such that $K$ and $L$ are separably closed and that $K$ has finite imperfectness degree. Then the following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The fields $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. \item The $K$-algebra $L$ is \'{e}tale. \item The extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary (in the language of rings). \item The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary. \item The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L_{e,m}$-elementary. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-fields such that $K$ and $L$ are separably closed and that $K$ has finite imperfectness degree
conclusions: the following are equivalent
equivalent_conditions: The fields $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis.
The extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary (in the language of rings).
nodes.label: elementaryetale

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: By the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Del1} and by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1}, the extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary if and only if $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. By \cite[Theorem 26.7]{mat}, it happens if and only if this extension is \'{e}tale, so we get the equivalence of $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$. \\ Since both the $\lambda$-function and the $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation are defined (over the field of the $p^m$-th powers) using the field operations and the elements of a $p$-basis, we get the equivalence of $(3)$ with $(4)$ and $(5)$.
nodes.statement_short: Delon's criterion and Matsumura 26.7 give (1)-(3); lambda and D are p-basis definable, giving (4),(5).

nodes.statement: By the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Del1} and by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1}, the extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary if and only if $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. By \cite[Theorem 26.7]{mat}, it happens if and only if this extension is \'{e}tale, so we get the equivalence of $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Delon and Matsumura give equivalence of (1)-(3).

nodes.statement: Since both the $\lambda$-function and the $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation are defined (over the field of the $p^m$-th powers) using the field operations and the elements of a $p$-basis, we get the equivalence of $(3)$ with $(4)$ and $(5)$.
nodes.statement_short: lambda and D are definable from a p-basis.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: We take the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^F$ on the field $K$ from Example \ref{canex}. By Proposition \ref{canstrict}, $\mathbf{K}$ is strict and clearly the imperfection degree of $K$ is $e$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $\mathbb{D}^F$ extends to the separable closure of $K$ (a separable algebraic extension is \'{e}tale, see \cite[Thm. 26.7]{mat}). By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(3), this extension is still strict. Since it is \'{e}tale, the degree of imperfection does not change.
nodes.statement_short: The canonical F-derivation on k((X)), extended to the separable closure, is a strict model of imperfection degree e.

nodes.name: Canonical F-field
nodes.statement: We take the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^F$ on the field $K$ from Example \ref{canex}. By Proposition \ref{canstrict}, $\mathbf{K}$ is strict and clearly the imperfection degree of $K$ is $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Take k((X)) with canonical F-derivation: strict, imperfection degree e.

nodes.name: Extend to separable closure
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $\mathbb{D}^F$ extends to the separable closure of $K$ (a separable algebraic extension is \'{e}tale, see \cite[Thm. 26.7]{mat}).
nodes.statement_short: Extend to the separable closure.

nodes.name: Still strict
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(3), this extension is still strict.
nodes.statement_short: Strictness persists.

nodes.name: Degree preserved
nodes.statement: Since it is \'{e}tale, the degree of imperfection does not change.
nodes.statement_short: Etale extension preserves imperfection degree.

nodes.name: Embedding into an elementary extension
nodes.statement: Let us take $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{F}$ being a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. Then there is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-embedding of $\mathbf{F}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$.
conclusions: there is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-embedding of $\mathbf{F}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$
nodes.label: elemamal

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{defgen}(1), Proposition \ref{etalegext} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(3), we can assume that $K$ is a field. By Lemma \ref{lamb}(1), we have $K^p=L^p\cap K$. Since $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and hence $\mathbf{K}$ is strict as well. By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(2), we can $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-amalgamate $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable, by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1} there is an elementary extension in the language of fields $L\preccurlyeq L'$ and a field embedding $\Upsilon:F'\to L'$ over $L$. The situation is described in the following diagram: \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{4pc} \xymatrix{ & & L'\\ & \mathbf{F}'\ar[ru]^{\Upsilon} & \\ \mathbf{F}\ar[ru]^{} & & \mathbf{L}\ar[lu]^{} \ar[uu]^{\preccurlyeq}\\ & \mathbf{K}\ar[ru]^{}\ar[lu]^{}. & } \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale. The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$ is strict, so by Corollary \ref{dimconstants}, we have $[F':(F')^p]\leqslant p^e$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable and $[L:L^p]=p^e$, by the equivalence between $(1)$ and $(2)$ in Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is \'{e}tale. Then the extension $F'\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale as well. By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $L'$ extending the one on $F'$ (hence also extending the one on $L$). By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $\mathbf{L}\subseteq \mathbf{L}'$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamate F and L over K, embed into an elementary field extension L' of L, and use etaleness to extend the g-derivation to L'.

nodes.name: K a field
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{defgen}(1), Proposition \ref{etalegext} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(3), we can assume that $K$ is a field.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG K is a field.

nodes.name: K strict
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lamb}(1), we have $K^p=L^p\cap K$. Since $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and hence $\mathbf{K}$ is strict as well.
nodes.statement_short: K inherits strictness from L.

nodes.name: Amalgamate
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(2), we can $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-amalgamate $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamate F and L over K into strict F'.

nodes.name: Embed in elementary extension
nodes.statement: Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable, by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1} there is an elementary extension in the language of fields $L\preccurlyeq L'$ and a field embedding $\Upsilon:F'\to L'$ over $L$. The situation is described in the following diagram: \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{4pc} \xymatrix{ & & L'\\ & \mathbf{F}'\ar[ru]^{\Upsilon} & \\ \mathbf{F}\ar[ru]^{} & & \mathbf{L}\ar[lu]^{} \ar[uu]^{\preccurlyeq}\\ & \mathbf{K}\ar[ru]^{}\ar[lu]^{}. & } \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Embed F' into an elementary field extension L' of L.

nodes.name: L' etale over L
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale.
nodes.statement_short: L' is etale over L.

nodes.name: F' etale over L
nodes.statement: The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$ is strict, so by Corollary \ref{dimconstants}, we have $[F':(F')^p]\leqslant p^e$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable and $[L:L^p]=p^e$, by the equivalence between $(1)$ and $(2)$ in Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is \'{e}tale. Then the extension $F'\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale as well.
nodes.statement_short: Degree count shows F' and hence L' etale over F'.

nodes.name: Extend derivation to L'
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $L'$ extending the one on $F'$ (hence also extending the one on $L$). By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $\mathbf{L}\subseteq \mathbf{L}'$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the g-derivation to L', an elementary extension of L.

nodes.name: Model companion of g-DF
nodes.statement: We have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ has quantifier elimination in the language $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$. \item Each model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ embeds into a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$. \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$. \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is a model completion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}_{\lambda}$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ has quantifier elimination in the language $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$.
Each model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ embeds into a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$.
The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$.
The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is a model completion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}_{\lambda}$.
nodes.statement_short: g-DCF_lambda eliminates quantifiers and is the model completion of g-DF_lambda; g-DCF is the model companion of g-DF.
nodes.label: qegdcf

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we use the criterion from \cite[Theorem 13.1]{sacks} (and Proposition \ref{elemamal}) exactly as in \cite[3.1]{Zieg2}. \\ For $(2)$, let us take any $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}$. By Proposition \ref{gstrictexist}, we may assume that $\mathbf{F}$ is strict. By Lemma \ref{consistent}, there is $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$. Clearly, $k$ with the trivial $\mathfrak{g}$-structure is a common $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. By Proposition \ref{elemamal}, $\mathbf{F}$ embeds into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$, which is clearly a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ as well. \\ By $(1)$, $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is model complete, so using Lemma \ref{lamb}(2) and Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, we get that $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is model complete as well. By $(2)$, $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$, so we get $(3)$. \\ By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and the item $(1)$, we get $(4)$.
nodes.statement_short: QE via Sacks' criterion and Proposition 4.4; embedding via strict extensions and consistency; model completeness transfers to g-DCF.

nodes.name: Part (1): QE
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we use the criterion from \cite[Theorem 13.1]{sacks} (and Proposition \ref{elemamal}) exactly as in \cite[3.1]{Zieg2}.
nodes.statement_short: Sacks' criterion with Proposition 4.4.

nodes.name: Part (2): embedding
nodes.statement: For $(2)$, let us take any $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}$. By Proposition \ref{gstrictexist}, we may assume that $\mathbf{F}$ is strict. By Lemma \ref{consistent}, there is $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$. Clearly, $k$ with the trivial $\mathfrak{g}$-structure is a common $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. By Proposition \ref{elemamal}, $\mathbf{F}$ embeds into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$, which is clearly a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to a strict extension and embed over k into an elementary extension of a model.

nodes.name: Part (3): model companion
nodes.statement: By $(1)$, $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is model complete, so using Lemma \ref{lamb}(2) and Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, we get that $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is model complete as well. By $(2)$, $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$, so we get $(3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Model completeness transfers to g-DCF; with (2) it is the model companion.

nodes.name: Part (4)
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and the item $(1)$, we get $(4)$.
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamation plus QE gives model completion.

nodes.name: Further properties and special cases of g-DCF
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ does not have the amalgamation property. The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ does not have quantifier elimination and the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is not a model completion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$. \item We have (after taking $k={\mathds{F}}_p$) $$\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}^e[m]-\mathrm{DCF} =\mathrm{SCH}_{p,e,m},$$ where $\mathrm{SCH}_{p,e,m}$ is the theory considered in \cite{K3}. \item If we take the algebraic group $U$ from Example \ref{gitex}(2), then a $U(1)$-field is the same as a field with two derivations $\partial_1,\partial_2$ such that $\partial_1^{(p)}=\partial_2$ and $\partial_2^{(p)}=0$. Hence $U(1)-\mathrm{DCF}$ corresponds to Wood's theory $2-\mathrm{DCF}$, see \cite{Wo2}. It should be possible to find algebraic groups governing the iterative rules for Wood's theories $m-\mathrm{DCF}$ for an arbitrary $m$. \item After dropping the iterativity assumptions rather strange things happen. In the case of characteristic zero, model companions exist and are analyzed in \cite{MS2}. In the case of positive characteristic, it is shown in \cite[Prop 7.2]{MS2} that (in our terminology) the theory of fields with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations has a model companion if and only if $m=1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: g-DF lacks AP; recovers SCH_{p,e,m} and Wood's 2-DCF; without iterativity model companions exist only for m=1.

nodes.statement: Let $L_e$ be the language of $k$-algebras with $e$-dimensional HS-derivations.

nodes.statement: Let $F-\mathrm{DF}$ be the theory of $F$-fields.

nodes.statement: Let $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ be the theory $F-\mathrm{DF}$ with the extra axioms for strict $F$-fields, and for separably closed fields of imperfection degree $e$.

nodes.name: Transport of g-derivations along ring isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $f\in \mathrm{Aut}(k)$ and let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an isomorphism of rings extending $f$. For any $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$, we define: $$\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}:S\to S[\mathbf{v}_m],\ \ \ \mathbb{D}^{\varphi}:=\varphi[\mathbf{v}_m]\circ \mathbb{D}\circ \varphi^{-1}.$$ Then $\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$-derivation, where $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$ is the group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ twisted by $f$.
assumptions: Let $f\in \mathrm{Aut}(k)$ and let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an isomorphism of rings extending $f$.
conclusions: $\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$-derivation

nodes.name: Smallest strict F-field extension
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}=(K,\mathbb{D})$ be an $F$-field. Then there is a smallest strict $F$-field extending $\mathbf{K}$.
conclusions: there is a smallest strict $F$-field extending $\mathbf{K}$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.8
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be the field of constants of $\mathbf{K}$. It is enough to show that there is a unique $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $C^{1/p}$ extending $\mathbb{D}$. By Lemma \ref{deronc}(1), $C$ is an $F$-subfield of $K$. For $\mathbf{i}\in {\mathds{N}}^e$ and $a\in C^{1/p}$, we have the only option (as in \cite[Lemma 2.4]{Zieg2}): $$D'_{\mathbf{i}}(a):=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(a^p))^{1/p}.$$ Clearly, each $D'_{\mathbf{i}}$ extends $D_{\mathbf{i}}$. We need to show that $\mathbb{D}'=(D'_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}\in {\mathds{N}}^e}$ is an $F$-derivation. By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2), the sequence of maps $$\mathbb{D}'':=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(b))_{\mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^e}$$ is an $F[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-derivation on $C$. It is easy to see that $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ coincides with $\mathbb{D}''$ ``transported'' to $C^{1/p}$ using the ring isomorphism $\mathrm{Fr}^{-1}_C:C\to C^{1/p}$. By Lemma \ref{transport}, $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ is an $F[m-1]$-derivation. Since it happens for all $m\in {\mathds{N}}$, we get that $\mathbb{D}'$ is an $F$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: Extend D to C^{1/p} by the only possible formula D'_i(a)=(D_{pi}(a^p))^{1/p}, checked truncation by truncation via transport.

nodes.name: Reduce to C^{1/p}
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be the field of constants of $\mathbf{K}$. It is enough to show that there is a unique $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $C^{1/p}$ extending $\mathbb{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: a unique F-derivation on C^{1/p} extending D.

nodes.name: C is an F-subfield
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{deronc}(1), $C$ is an $F$-subfield of $K$.
nodes.statement_short: C is an F-subfield.

nodes.name: Only possible formula
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{i}\in {\mathds{N}}^e$ and $a\in C^{1/p}$, we have the only option (as in \cite[Lemma 2.4]{Zieg2}): $$D'_{\mathbf{i}}(a):=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(a^p))^{1/p}.$$ Clearly, each $D'_{\mathbf{i}}$ extends $D_{\mathbf{i}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define D'_i(a)=(D_{pi}(a^p))^{1/p}.

nodes.name: Induced F[m-1]^Fr-derivation
nodes.statement: We need to show that $\mathbb{D}'=(D'_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}\in {\mathds{N}}^e}$ is an $F$-derivation. By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2), the sequence of maps $$\mathbb{D}'':=(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(b))_{\mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^e}$$ is an $F[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-derivation on $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.31(2) gives an F[m-1]^Fr-derivation on C.

nodes.name: Transport
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ coincides with $\mathbb{D}''$ ``transported'' to $C^{1/p}$ using the ring isomorphism $\mathrm{Fr}^{-1}_C:C\to C^{1/p}$. By Lemma \ref{transport}, $\mathbb{D}'[m-1]$ is an $F[m-1]$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: Transport via inverse Frobenius (Lemma 4.7).

nodes.name: All truncations
nodes.statement: Since it happens for all $m\in {\mathds{N}}$, we get that $\mathbb{D}'$ is an $F$-derivation.
nodes.statement_short: Holds for all m, so D' is an F-derivation.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.9
nodes.statement: Proceeding similarly as in the proof of \cite[Prop. 2.6]{Zieg2} (or Proposition \ref{lambdaap}) and using Proposition \ref{strictext} one shows the following.

nodes.statement: We can conclude now as in Section \ref{sececg}.

nodes.name: F-DCF is the model completion of F-DF
nodes.statement: The theory $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model completion of the theory $F-\mathrm{DF}$ (so it eliminates quantifiers).
conclusions: The theory $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model completion of the theory $F-\mathrm{DF}$ (so it eliminates quantifiers).

nodes.name: Smallest strict extensions give QE and elimination of imaginaries
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The extra property which makes the theory $F-\mathrm{DF}$ nicer than the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ is the existence of the \emph{smallest} strict extensions (Proposition \ref{strictext}). It gives the amalgamation property for \emph{all} (i.e. not necessarily strict) $F$-fields (Proposition \ref{apf}) and the quantifier elimination for $F-\mathrm{DCF}$. \item In this context, quantifier elimination for $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ implies elimination of imaginaries for $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ exactly as in Section 4 of \cite{Zieg2}. \end{enumerate}

$$F-\mathrm{DCF} = \bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}F[m]-\mathrm{DCF}.$$

nodes.statement: In this subsection, we discuss the opposite problem: can any model of $\mathrm{SCF}_{p,e}$ be expanded to a model of $F-\mathrm{DCF}$? The same question can be asked for $\mathfrak{g}$ in place of $F$.

nodes.name: Language L and theory SCF_{p,e}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.14
nodes.statement: Take $x_1,\ldots,x_e\in k(G)$ as in Lemma \ref{finsep}, denote $(x_1,\ldots,x_e)$ by $\mathbf{x}$ and let $y\in k(G)$ be separable algebraic over $k(\mathbf{x})$ such that $k(\mathbf{x},y)=k(G)$ (such $y$ exists by Lemma \ref{finsep} and Abel's theorem). Then for any $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in {\mathds{N}}^e$, there are polynomials $F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}},H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}\in k[\mathbf{X},Y]$ such that for the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^{F}=(D_{\mathbf{j}}^F)_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{N}^e}$ on $k(G)$, we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}^F(\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{i}})=\frac{F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{x},y)}{H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{x},y)}\in k(G).$$ We describe now an extension by definitions of the theory $\mathrm{SCF}_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ coinciding with the theory $G-\mathrm{DCF}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$. To ease the notation, we will also denote by $\mathbf{b}$ the tuple (of constant symbols or elements of a model) $(b_1,\ldots,b_e)$. Take $\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_e)\in\mathbb{N}^e$, for every $n\geqslant \max\lbrace j_1,\ldots,j_e\rbrace$ we add to the theory $\mathrm{SCF}_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$ the following defining axiom \begin{equation}\tag{$\clubsuit$} D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)=y \leftrightarrow \left(\exists^{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\; \alpha_{\mathbf{i}}\right) \left(x=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\alpha_{\mathbf{i}}^{p^n}\mathbf{b}^{\mathbf{i}} \;\wedge\; y=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{i}\in[p^n]^e}\alpha_{\mathbf{i}}^{p^n}\frac{F_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{b},c)}{H_{\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{b},c)} \right). \end{equation} Take any $(K,\mathbf{b},c)\models \mathrm{SCF}_{p,e}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$. It is not hard to verify that the defining axioms (\ref{scfD}) determine well-defined functions on $K$. The axioms $\beta,\gamma$ guarantee that $$k(\mathbf{b},c)\cong_k k(G)$$ and that $\mathbb{D}:=(D_{\mathbf{j}})_{\mathbf{j}\in {\mathds{N}}^e}$ restricted to $k(\mathbf{b},c)$ corresponds to the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$. Because $\mathbf{b}$ is a $p$-basis of $K$, the extension $k(\mathbf{b})\subseteq K$ is \'{e}tale (see \cite[Theorem 26.8]{mat}). Hence the extension $k(\mathbf{b},c)\subseteq K$ is also \'{e}tale. Due to Proposition \ref{etalehs}, we can extend the canonical $G$-derivation from $k(G)$ to the field $K$. Let $\mathbb{D}'=\left(D'_{\mathbf{j}}\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in\mathbb{N}^e}$ denote the $G$-derivation on $K$ extending the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$. Note that $D'_{\mathbf{j}}(x)=D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)$ for every $x\in K$, hence $\mathbb{D}'=\mathbb{D}$. Moreover the canonical $G$-derivation on $k(G)$ is strict, so also $\mathbb{D}'|_{k(\mathbf{b},c)}$ is strict. Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} implies that $\mathbb{D}'=\mathbb{D}$ is strict, so $(K,\mathbb{D},\mathbf{b},c)\models G-\mathrm{DCF}^{{\mathbf{b}},c}$.

nodes.name: e.c. implies axioms
nodes.statement: Assume that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field. Then by Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $K$ is separably closed (since a separable algebraic field extension is \'{e}tale). Take any $K$-irreducible $K$-varieties $V\subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$, $W\subseteq \nabla(V)$ and $Z\subsetneq W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$ then there is $b_0\in\Omega^n$ and $b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{p^{me}-1})\in\Omega^{np^{me}}$ such that $V=\mathrm{locus}_K(b_0)$ and $W=\mathrm{locus}_K(b)$. Since $c_V(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$, Lemma \ref{cVW} implies that there exists a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (K(b),\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$. We have $$\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b\in W(K(b))\setminus Z(K(b))$$ and $b_0\in V(K(b))$. Since $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is existentially closed, there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}_V(b'_0)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Existentially closed fields satisfy the geometric axioms.

nodes.name: Separably closed
nodes.statement: Assume that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field. Then by Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $K$ is separably closed (since a separable algebraic field extension is \'{e}tale).
nodes.statement_short: K is separably closed by etale extension.

nodes.name: Generic points
nodes.statement: Take any $K$-irreducible $K$-varieties $V\subseteq \mathbb{A}^n$, $W\subseteq \nabla(V)$ and $Z\subsetneq W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$ then there is $b_0\in\Omega^n$ and $b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{p^{me}-1})\in\Omega^{np^{me}}$ such that $V=\mathrm{locus}_K(b_0)$ and $W=\mathrm{locus}_K(b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take generic points b_0, b of V, W.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement: Since $c_V(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$, Lemma \ref{cVW} implies that there exists a $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (K(b),\mathbb{D}')$ such that $\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.5 gives a g-field extension with D'_V(b_0)=b.

nodes.name: Point in extension
nodes.statement: We have $$\mathbb{D}'_V(b_0)=b\in W(K(b))\setminus Z(K(b))$$ and $b_0\in V(K(b))$.
nodes.statement_short: b lies in W minus Z in the extension.

nodes.name: Pull back
nodes.statement: Since $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is existentially closed, there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}_V(b'_0)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Existential closedness gives such a point in K.

nodes.name: Axioms imply e.c.
nodes.statement: Assume now that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is a model of the ``geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$'' and let $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (L,\mathbb{D}')$ be an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields. Take any quantifier-free formula $\varphi(x_0,\ldots,x_{p^{me}-1})$ over $K$ (in the language of fields), where each $x_i$ is an $n$-tuple of variables for an arbitrary (but fixed) positive integer $n$. Suppose that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(x_0))$. Take $b_0\in L^n$ such that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(b_0))$ and set $$V=\mathrm{locus}_K(b_0),\ \ b=\mathbb{D}_V'(b_0),\ \ W=\mathrm{locus}_K(b),\ \ Z_0=\lbrace d\in W\;\;|\;\; \neg\varphi(d)\rbrace.$$ Let $Z$ denote the intersection of all $K$-subvarieties of $W$ containing $Z_0$. Clearly $b\in W(L)\setminus Z(L)$ and the second condition of Lemma \ref{cVW} is satisfied, so $c_{V}(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$. Hence all the assumptions of the ``geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$'' hold. Therefore there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}(b_0')\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$ and $(K,\mathbb{D})\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}(x_0))$.
nodes.statement_short: Models of the geometric axioms are existentially closed.

nodes.name: Extension L
nodes.statement: Assume now that $(K,\mathbb{D})$ is a model of the ``geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$'' and let $(K,\mathbb{D})\subseteq (L,\mathbb{D}')$ be an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields.
nodes.statement_short: Take a g-field extension L.

nodes.name: Encode formula
nodes.statement: Take any quantifier-free formula $\varphi(x_0,\ldots,x_{p^{me}-1})$ over $K$ (in the language of fields), where each $x_i$ is an $n$-tuple of variables for an arbitrary (but fixed) positive integer $n$. Suppose that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(x_0))$. Take $b_0\in L^n$ such that $(L,\mathbb{D}')\models\varphi(\mathbb{D}'(b_0))$ and set $$V=\mathrm{locus}_K(b_0),\ \ b=\mathbb{D}_V'(b_0),\ \ W=\mathrm{locus}_K(b),\ \ Z_0=\lbrace d\in W\;\;|\;\; \neg\varphi(d)\rbrace.$$
nodes.statement_short: Encode an existential formula realized in L by loci V, W and Z_0.

nodes.name: Check hypotheses
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ denote the intersection of all $K$-subvarieties of $W$ containing $Z_0$. Clearly $b\in W(L)\setminus Z(L)$ and the second condition of Lemma \ref{cVW} is satisfied, so $c_{V}(W)\subseteq \nabla(W)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.5 gives c_V(W) in nabla(W).

nodes.name: Axioms apply
nodes.statement: Hence all the assumptions of the ``geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$'' hold.
nodes.statement_short: The geometric axioms apply.

nodes.name: Realize in K
nodes.statement: Therefore there is $b_0'\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}(b_0')\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$ and $(K,\mathbb{D})\models (\exists x_0)\varphi(\mathbb{D}(x_0))$.
nodes.statement_short: So the formula is realized in K.

nodes.name: Section 4 results not used for Theorem 5.6
nodes.statement: Note that the results of Section \ref{secmc} are not used in the proof of Theorem \ref{ggeo} which suggests a possibility of generalizations, e.g. to the context of $\mathcal{D}$-fields from \cite{MS}.
nodes.label: gremark

nodes.name: Geometric axioms for F-DCF as a union
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{chain}, the geometric axioms for $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ are given as the union (over $m$) of the geometric axioms for $F[m]-\mathrm{DCF}$.
conclusions: the geometric axioms for $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ are given as the union (over $m$) of the geometric axioms for $F[m]-\mathrm{DCF}$

nodes.name: Geometric axioms for F-DCF
nodes.statement:
We state these axioms explicitly below, where $
abla_m$ denotes the functor $
abla$ with respect to $\mathbb{D}[m]$ (similarly for $c_m$). \ \ { f Geometric axioms for $F-\mathrm{DCF}$}  egin{enumerate} \item The field $K$ is separably closed. \item For any positive integers $n,m$, suppose that $V\subseteq {\mathbb A}^n$ and $W\subseteq 
abla_m(V)$ are absolutely irreducible $K$-varieties, and $Z$ is a proper $K$-subvariety of $W$. If $W$ projects generically onto $V$, and $c_{m,V}(W)\subseteq 
abla_m(W)$, then there is $a\in V(K)$ such that $\mathbb{D}[m]_{V}(a)\in W(K)\setminus Z(K)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Geometric axioms for F-DCF
nodes.statement: The $F$-field $\mathbf{K}$ is an existentially closed $F$-field if and only if $\mathbf{K}$ is a model of the geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$.
conclusions: The $F$-field $\mathbf{K}$ is an existentially closed $F$-field if and only if $\mathbf{K}$ is a model of the geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$.
equivalent_conditions: $\mathbf{K}$ is a model of the geometric axioms for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$
nodes.label: fgeo

nodes.name: Theorem 4.12 is needed for Theorem 5.8
nodes.statement: Unlike in the proof of Theorem \ref{ggeo}, the results of Section \ref{secmc} \emph{are} used for the proof of Theorem \ref{fgeo}, since Theorem \ref{chain} is necessary for the geometric axiomatization and the proof of Theorem \ref{chain} requires the algebraic axiomatizations of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ and $F-\mathrm{DCF}$. However, one can also prove Theorem \ref{chain} (but for a limited class of formal groups $F$ only) in another fashion as it was done in \cite{K3} for $F=\widehat{\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}^e}$. This approach will be discussed in Section \ref{secgtup}.
nodes.label: fremark

nodes.name: Extension to iterative D-fields of positive characteristic
nodes.statement: One could wonder whether our techniques may be generalized to include the case of iterative $\underline{\mathcal{D}}$-fields of positive characteristic. It seems likely in the case where an iterative system $(\underline{\mathcal{D}},\Delta)$ is the inverse limit of finite iterative systems $(\mathcal{D}_m,\Delta_m)_m$ resembling the ones given by Hopf algebra comultiplications $\mu_m:\mathcal{D}_m\to \mathcal{D}_m\circ \mathcal{D}_m$ (see Section \ref{secproco}). More precisely, our techniques may apply to the iterative systems $(\underline{\mathcal{D}},\Delta)$ where each morphism $\Delta_{p^m}:\mathcal{D}_{2p^m}\to \mathcal{D}_{p^m}\circ \mathcal{D}_{p^m}$ factors through the projection morphism $\mathcal{D}_{2p^m}\to \mathcal{D}_{p^m}$.
assumptions: an iterative system $(\underline{\mathcal{D}},\Delta)$ is the inverse limit of finite iterative systems $(\mathcal{D}_m,\Delta_m)_m$
conclusions: our techniques may apply to the iterative systems $(\underline{\mathcal{D}},\Delta)$

nodes.name: Geometric axiomatization of existentially closed (D_m,Delta_m)-fields
nodes.statement: A geometric axiomatization of the class of existentially closed $(\mathcal{D}_m,\Delta_m)$-fields should not be very difficult, see Remark \ref{gremark}.
conclusions: should not be very difficult

nodes.name: Canonical G-tuple
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{D}$ be a $G[m]$-derivation on $K$. A subset $B\subseteq K$ is called a \emph{canonical $G$-tuple}, if $|B|=e$ and there is a $G[m]$-embedding $(k(G),\mathbb{D}[m]^G)\to \mathbf{K}$ such that $B$ is the image of the set of canonical parameters of $G$, where $\mathbb{D}[m]^G$ is the canonical $G[m]$-derivation from Example \ref{cangex}.
differentia: there is a $G[m]$-embedding $(k(G),\mathbb{D}[m]^G)\to \mathbf{K}$ such that $B$ is the image of the set of canonical parameters of $G$
nodes.label: defpbasis

nodes.name: Canonical G-tuples are p-bases
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and of imperfection degree $e$, then any canonical $G$-tuple in $L$ is a $p$-basis. For $G=\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}^e$, we recover the notion of a \emph{canonical $p$-basis} from \cite{Zieg2}.
nodes.label: geotuple

nodes.name: Existence of canonical G-tuples
nodes.statement: We say that \emph{canonical $G$-tuples exist} if for any $m$ and any separably closed $G[m]$-field $\mathbf{L}$, whenever $[L:C_L]=p^e$, there is a canonical $G$-tuple in $L$.
nodes.label: existence

nodes.name: Canonical G-bases for group scheme actions; known existence results
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Definition \ref{defpbasis} can be phrased in a (much) greater generality using group scheme actions. Let $\mathfrak{G}_0$ be a group subscheme of a group scheme $\mathfrak{G}$. Assume that $\mathfrak{G}_0$ acts (as a group scheme) on a scheme $V$. We say that this action has a \emph{canonical $\mathfrak{G}$-basis}, if there is an $\mathfrak{G}_0$-invariant morphism $V\to \mathfrak{G}$ such that the induced map $$V\to \mathfrak{G}\times_{\mathfrak{G}/\mathfrak{G}_0}V/\mathfrak{G}_0$$ is an isomorphism. \item The existence of canonical $\mathbb{G}_a^e$-tuples is shown in \cite{Zieg2} and the existence of canonical $\mathbb{G}_m$-tuples is shown in \cite{HK1}. Combining these results, one can show the existence of canonical $G$-tuples for $G$ of the form $\mathbb{G}_a^e\times\mathbb{G}_m^f$. \item We do not attack here the problem of the \emph{existence} of canonical $G$-tuples for a given algebraic group $G$. This will be done in \cite{Hoff1} (as well as possible applications to the notion of ``$G$-thinness''). \item The existence of canonical $G$-tuples implies (\emph{strong}) \emph{integrability} of $G$-derivations, as in (morally) \cite{Mats1} or as in \cite{HK1} (see also \cite{Tyc}) \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: greater

nodes.name: Canonical G-tuples give another proof of Theorem 4.12
nodes.statement: The existence of canonical $G$-tuples gives rather directly (see \cite[Thm. 2.3]{K3}) another proof of Theorem \ref{chain} which is the only ingredient needed in Section \ref{secaxioms} requiring specific differential-algebraic arguments.
